newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian prime minister to visit Russia this month.
newsitem.headline: Indian prime minister to visit Russia this month.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda will meet Russian President Boris Yeltsin during his first official visit to Moscow on March 24-26, a government spokesman said on Monday.
Deve Gowda, who assumed power at the head of a centre-left coalition last June, had scrapped a trip set for last month because Yeltsin was recovering from double pneumonia after heart surgery.

A controversial nuclear power project in southern India was expected to figure in Deve Gowda's talks in Moscow, analysts said. Other areas that could be discussed include trade, defence sales and New Delhi's bid for a permanent U.N. Security Council seat.

Last month, Washington urged Russia to drop its planned sale of two light-water nuclear reactors to India, saying it violated an international agreement and would set back a global effort to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.
The reactors, to be installed in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu, can produce 1,000 megawatts each.
Light-water reactors use ordinary water to slow down the neutrons emitted by nuclear fission to the speed required to sustain the chain reaction.
U.S. officials said Russia had signed an international agreement in 1992 forbidding it from exporting nuclear technology to aspiring nuclear nations.
Sales are forbidden to countries not formally recognised as nuclear weapons states and which do not allow international inspections of key nuclear institutes.
Only the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China are recognised as nuclear weapons states.
Russian officials insisted the sale to India should be exempted from the agreement because it was included in a 1987 understanding between then president Mikhail Gorbachev and Indian leaders.
Indian analysts accused the United States, which they said had agreed to supply two light-water reactors of 1,000 megawatts each to North Korea, of adopting a double standard.
India exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but says it has never built the bomb. New Delhi has refused to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty banning nuclear test blasts.
During the Cold War, the former Soviet Union and India nurtured close ties. Moscow was India's biggest arms supplier and an important trade partner.
After the demise of the Soviet Union, trade tapered off, choked by India's large unpaid debt. But both sides have sought to expand economic relations, and India remains an arms buyer.
Last month, the U.S. Defense News journal said India had agreed to buy two Kilo-class diesel submarines from Russia, although Deve Gowda's cabinet has not signed off on the deal.
In November, India signed a contract to buy up to 50 Russian Sukhoi SU-30 MK fighter jets worth more than $1 billion. India has yet to start taking delivery of the jets.
Apart from defence sales, the prime minister might also look for Moscow's support for New Delhi's bid to become a permanent member of the U.N. security council.
During a visit by Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov to New Delhi in October, both sides pledged to strengthen cooperation in the metallurgical and power sectors and boost trade.
